title: A signal detection theory approach to quantify contextual effects on perceived signal
abstract: The perceived value of a sensory stimulus is influenced by its surround. A classic visual example of such contextual effect is simultaneous brightness contrast, where the perceived brightness of a target patch is altered by the luminance of its background. Here, we propose a signal detection theory (SDT) based approach to quantify how context parameters bias perception. We develop an extension of SDT in which we formalize contextual effects as either additive or multiplicative gains on the internal representation of a stimulus within a two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task. The model generates clear, testable predictions: additive gains shift the point of subjective equality without altering the slope of the psychometric function, while multiplicative gains affect both its shift and slope. We use this framework to characterize contextual effects in a brightness discrimination experiment where observers compare the brightness of two achromatic patches on different achromatic backgrounds. Within the range of luminance conditions tested, the background produced an approximately constant shift of the point of subjective equality, which within our model corresponds to an additive rather than a multiplicative gain. This SDT-based paradigm provides a powerful and generalizable method for quantifying contextual effects in perception.
